utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. I read the Prosecution notice for the -- of witnesses for the next week. I take it from the fact that Mr. Van Lynden is scheduled to come back on Monday that it has been agreed by the parties that, Mr. Karadzic, you will conclude your cross-examination by today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much -- how much would you need for your redirect, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Not more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are several matters to deal with on the part of the Chamber at the end of today's session, so, Mr. Karadzic, I would like you to bear in your mind to conclude at least 40 minutes before the end of today's session. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to say good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, yesterday we showed what we had undertaken as our obligation at the London Conference and how we reacted, and I'm glad that you noticed that I did what I said I would do three days after our meeting. Now I would like to see 65 ter 01559 - this is a Prosecution document - to see what our army did in terms of our obligations from the conference. This is a document of the 6th of June, after the Lisbon conference where we were together. This is one of those notorious directives by General Mladic, so let's see what General Mladic ordered and how he understood things. This is a directive for further actions, dated the 6th of June, 1992. In the first paragraph it says: "The enemy started a general offence in the direction of Sarajevo." And the last sentence in that paragraph states: "The operation is intended to be carried out in the next five to six days in order to create favourable conditions for possible negotiations about demarcation in the broader area of Sarajevo." Paragraph 2: "The military of the Serbian Republic of B and H received the task to use offensive actions with the restricted objective of improving the operational tactical position in the broader area of Sarajevo ..." And then paragraph 4, the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the English it's on the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "I have decided with a persistent defence to defend the achieved lines." And then: "The goal of the action, secure parts of Sarajevo with a majority Serbian population, mop up or cleanse the broader area ..." Now, a new page in the Serbian. "... the broader area of the Sarajevo airport, and mop up or cleanse its wider area of remaining groups and of individuals belonging to the enemy, thus ensuring the safety needed to bring in -- for aircraft's bringing in humanitarian aid and render possible the normal supply of food and medication to the civilian population." And then C: "Open the following roads for the traffic: Sarajevo, Trnovo, Kalinovik, in order to provide regular supplies of humanitarian aid to the population." If you recall, we had agreed to have humanitarian aid deliveries through Metkovic as well. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. It's in the documents. We took it upon ourselves that we would open the Metkovic route through Eastern Herzegovina, and Mladic is ordering the security of that communication here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page is both in English and Serbian. Actually, we need to look at page 4 in the English. Where it says: "The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps ..." Last sentence: "Secure the communication -- the broader area of the airport to ensure the safe arrival of humanitarian aid." Then 6, paragraph 2, can we look at the next page in the English, please. "I strictly forbid the abuse of the civilian unarmed population and treat the prisoners in the spirit of the Geneva Conventions."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this more or less in accordance with what we agreed in Lisbon at the end of May, Colonel, sir? If you recall, I signed a statement which we can show. I signed it in Lisbon. I signed it there from which all the instructions issued by Mladic arise.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact details of -- as is portrayed in this letter, which -- which I'm totally unaware of. My understanding of the main achievement in Lisbon was as a consequence of the mortar attack on the bread queue in Sarajevo that we secured your general agreement for the consideration of handing the airport over to the United Nations. That's the main achievement, as I recall. These are all details of a letter that was sent out by a general. It doesn't mean very much to me. I'd like to see the spirit of it going into being implemented rather than just being written in a letter. So I have no knowledge of this letter. I have no knowledge of the details. And, therefore, I have no further comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, you can comment on everything when it's in favour of the Prosecution, but when the Defence is putting something evident to you, what do you think about what I'm saying to you now? Colonel, sir, you are quite partial now. This is not a letter. This is an order, a directive, which must not be understood as a letter. It has to be executed. Whoever knows Mladic knows that this had to be executed. And the fact that a shell forced me -- well, this is quite partial, Colonel. Since you don't know anything of the things that I was ordering, do you recall the directive of the 12th of April? How can you be so partial, and why are you so partial? Can you explain this to everybody?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm simply saying, Mr. Karadzic, is that you have produced a plethora of documents allegedly giving directives. What I'm saying to you is I have no proof as to whether the contents of those directives were obeyed. It's as simple as that. I have never seen any of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. I asked you whether the contents of this directive are in accordance with what I stated and signed in Lisbon.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm saying to you that I do not know the exact content of everything that was agreed in Lisbon. If you can produce the document that was signed, then I might be in a position of commenting on it. I don't recall its exact detail, except the portion which emphasised the need for the airport to be handed over to the United Nations in order to provide humanitarian assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How can you say, Colonel, sir, that a shell forced me to do it when it was something that I proposed even before the conference and when you know about my platform of the 22nd of April? We have been listening your quite partial testimony for the past three days when you say, Yes, but the Serbs did something in Zvornik. But you don't know what was actually going on in Zvornik. You have to be aware that the Defence considers you to be a completely partial witness who is defending himself. I'm not attacking you. I'm asking for your knowledge, your conclusions. I'm asking for what you know about the events as somebody who was actually there. Yes, you can tell us what you are thinking. I am just saying that you are evading to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put your question one at a time instead of making a long speech. Mr. Doyle, you are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm simply saying that my recollection of what was discussed in Lisbon was only achieved after the attack of the mortar, the mortar attack in Sarajevo. Up to that time, there was no progress made on anything. And it was a consequence of that mortar attack that the chairman of the peace talks, Mr. Cutileiro, persuaded Mr. Karadzic to give something out of that conference that would be of some benefit. And that is my clear recollection. All of these details that are in this letter I'm certainly not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, you will agree that the 17th of May came before the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document, Your Honours, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will -- unless it is objected to, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit Number D232.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] can we now look at 1D891 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, sir, this is my letter to Ambassador Cutileiro of the 17th of May, and you will see that the Serbian side is constantly making initiatives, and you are saying that I was forced to do something by a bomb which we didn't fire, and it's not in my indictment, and I can prove that we did not fire it. Here is the letter, sir. For example, we would like to keep you properly informed about the situation [In English] in Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly in Sarajevo. The war is getting worse and worse, and it is turning into a disaster. We have made many peaceful proposals directly to the Muslim side and UNPROFOR, but there was no response but more and more fire. Finally our Assembly," excuse me. "Finally our Assembly declared a unilateral cease-fire, and it expires tomorrow, May the 18th. Our unilateral cease-fair was understood as our weakness, and we were attacked even more savagely. In spite of talks and at the time the talks were being held, Mr. Izetbegovic made two statements in two days that they were going to victory, until they clean Bosnia from terrorists. By terrorists, he meant Serbs. His statement sounds -- sounded as a call for jihad. Today next-door neighbours in the Serbian suburbs of Pofalici killed at least 50 Serbs." [Interpretation] To correct this, 250 Serbs. We knew at that point in time that Colonel, sir, 250 Serbs were killed in Pofalici at that time, and that was the only Serbian settlement we were not controlling. At least 50 Serbs. But some estimation make it 200. "[In English] Every day, Muslims make savage attacks on Serbian municipalities, particularly on Ilidza, and Serbs never attacked Muslim municipalities. As far as the Croatian side is concerned, Kupres is quiet. The situation in the Neretva valley is better but not good. [No interpretation] [In English] In Bosanski Brod, Croatian regulars has doubled armed forces and chasing Serbs out of this municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we look at the last page, please, page 2. Ah, we can stay on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Mr. Izetbegovic does not want this conference anymore. He is asking for foreign military help from Islamic countries. We have strong evidence that Libya is involved and that it is the only country which has its consulate in Sarajevo. Turkey, Egypt, Morocco, and other Islamic countries are getting interested in the outcome of the Bosnian crisis. If the conference does not continue, the war will become even more terrible, and it will not stop until the side is - next - is completely defeated. As you know, all my predictions have become true, and I am not happy about it. So we propose unconditional resumption of the conference. If it is conditioned by cease-fire, that means that Mr. Izetbegovic will have a way to hinder and sabotage it as long as he wants to do it." [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, may I remind you of the directive of -- actually, the platform of the 22nd of April, and would I like to ask you if you have anything of our statements or declarations to show that was warmongering and that was against a political resolution of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any documentation, and I would just say for -- during that period that was made out, I was in the United Kingdom. I wasn't in Bosnia. So I don't have any knowledge of the content of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't -- that's -- you were not in Sarajevo on the 27th of April, but in Lisbon. But you know that a bomb influenced me. Colonel, sir, you are partial, and you can see that from the moon. By the 22nd of May we had made these proposals, but the shell fell on the 27th of May. This was on the 17th. It was five days after you arrived. But you knew what was going on; you were in Lisbon, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the accused is arguing with the witness. He's not really asking questions any more. He's making statements and arguing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To a certain extent. Mr. Doyle, if you could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I'm saying in relation to this is that if this is a letter that was made out on the 17th of May, I was not in Bosnia on the 17th of May. I had left on the 12th of May when I was evacuated from the city of Sarajevo and between then and the time that I returned home on the 1st of October I was in Bosnia on three occasions. I was with Mr. Cutileiro for the talks in Lisbon, yes. I recalled the general content of the agreement that was attained in Lisbon, yes. But in relation to this letter, I have no knowledge of, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, Colonel, do you have any idea at all of its content, any idea at all of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, of this letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: No idea at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then, Colonel, if you have no knowledge of that, why then do you not withdraw your allegations and those additions you made to your answer -- in your answers to questions I didn't ask you? How can you say, if you have no knowledge and awareness of this and if you weren't informed properly in the conference where you took part as Lord Carrington's representative, why are you stating that a shell forced me to be humane and peace-loving?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, Mr. Karadzic, I've already explained under testimony as to what the consequences of that mortar shell was on the peace talks in Lisbon. You may recall that as soon as this occurred, Mr. Silajdzic came into the conference and informed Mr. Cutileiro that because of this mortar attack, which everybody saw on international television, he saw there was no use to continue the talks. He said he was leaving. And then you come in a short time later to inform the conference or to inform those of us who were there that the Serbs were not responsible for the mortar attack on the bread queue. Mr. Cutileiro was of the view that if the talks were to be suspended without any progress, this would not look well; and, therefore, he suggested to you that as a gesture and that if you were to give under certain conditions an assurance that the airport of Sarajevo would be handed over to the United Nations, that would be a positive outcome of the talks, and that's what was achieved. Nobody is saying who fired the mortar bomb. I don't know who fired it. I've already said that in testimony yesterday. I assumed the United Nations, who had a large contingent of troops in the city and would have done a crater analysis would be a better judge to make that call. I do not know. I don't have an answer for it. So I have nothing further to say on that mortar attack, except that the conference exploited that attack to get you to give an undertaking that under certain circumstances you would be agreeable to hand over the airport to the United Nations to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know, Colonel, that I proposed that even earlier and that we were always in favour of having humanitarian aid delivered?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, in the meantime, I'll find that statement of mine made in Lisbon that I gave unilaterally. But do you see this directive of General Mladic's, Colonel, both from -- the one from June -- well, that one's been adopted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can I have Prosecution Exhibit 1600 up next, please. The previous document has been admitted; right? Is the directive in evidence? Well, it's a letter actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think so. Let's -- it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D233, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have Prosecution 65 ter 1600 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is also one of Mladic's directives for further action on the 8th of August, which completely reflects the continuity of his efforts to ensure that humanitarian deliveries arrive. Now, let me ask you first, Colonel. You said that Silajdzic arrived and that he used the mortar to interrupt the conference. Now, we claim and state that all those incidents were geared towards stopping the conference, because they were offered the whole of Bosnia. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that to me is -- is an opinion being expressed by you, and that's fine by me. It's not the opinion that I would have. I agree with you when you say that the conference -- the main reason why the conference was stopped was because of this attack which took place in Sarajevo. Yes, I am in agreement with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you also agree that the Serbs didn't want the conference to be stopped, whereas the Muslims did? And that you never had to prevail upon the Serbs to attend the conference, whereas you did have to persuade the Muslims to do so?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any occasion when I had to persuade the Muslims to attend a conference, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says in your diary. You had to persuade the HDZ and SDA to go to the conference, and we looked at that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. I've already explained that the reason why we had to persuade the president to go was because he thought he would be killed by Bosnian Serbs on his way to the airport. It wasn't a question of his unwillingness to attend the conference. It was his concern about his own safety in getting to the airport. No more than that. It was a security measure and a matter of safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May we now have a look at this directive from General Mladic from August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Partly due to the accused's habit of asking multiple questions, but how about the first part of his question, whether you would agree that Serbs didn't want the conference to be stopped, whereas the Muslims did. What is your observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I -- my only observation is, I don't know if any side wanted the conference to cease. I don't know if any side took efforts to ensure the conference would cease, so I don't have a -- I don't have an answer for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, can we just for a moment look at another document, and we'll come back to this one. It is 65 ter 05875, 05875, just for a brief moment, and then we'll get back to the directive. It's my letter to Ambassador Cutileiro, dated the 5th of June. And that's the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we turn to the second page, please. This is the Serbian version. The second page in English, please. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Dear Mr. Cutileiro. "Tonight, the 5th of June, Mr. Izetbegovic gave a negative reply to Lord Carrington's letter about the conference on Bosnia. On the news, television news, he explicitly said," and I quote, "that now everything is different and that he does not want any conference about the constituent units." Those are his words. "Despite the goodwill we showed in our readiness to open the airport unconditionally," unconditionally I repeat, "we were blackmailed with the lives of JNA families to leave the heavy arms in the Marsal Tito Barracks. That same evening the Muslim side started shelling Serb residential areas in Sarajevo. "We hope that you can still mediate and bring the Muslim side to the conference. However, we have to know the truth because the Serbian people feel both tricked and in jeopardy. Namely, if you cannot keep your promises, publicly announced and confirmed by the European Community, we have to protect the Serbian people on their ethnic territories." And it is to be sent to Lord Carrington, forwarded to Lord Carrington, as well. Do you know that Mr. Izetbegovic, in the television news, said that he was no longer interested in any conference about constituent units and that everything was different now, and that was his permanent position, that the conference was to be avoided? First of all, do you know that he said that? Let's take that first.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no personal knowledge that he said that, Mr. Karadzic, but I'm sure Mr. Cutileiro might be in a better position, because the letter was addressed to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, I have a problem here with witnesses. Not only with you but some others too. With all due respect, it would be better if your bosses came in to testify then because you know nothing about the conference. You know nothing about the conference, and yet you were a participant and this letter is important. And you're testifying as an eyewitness and a participant and yet you say you know nothing. How come you know nothing about this? Did you follow the conference? Were you a participant and associate of Lord Carrington's or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assisting the peace conference on Yugoslavia based on my experience and my service as head of the monitor mission in whatever capacity it was felt I might be able to make a contribution. If you deem that not to be sufficient, that's your choice, Mr. Karadzic. But I'm trying to give a truthful account of what I did, what I didn't, what I saw, and what I didn't, and beyond that I really do not have any comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you see Zvornik and Foca and that's what you're testifying about?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see Zvornik and Foca. I repeated earlier that I was given the content of a verbal report from the monitor mission who attempted to get to Foca. And I was given the content of a verbal report given to me by Mr. Martin Bell of the BBC in relation to Zvornik, and I believe that's what I said here under testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you were in Sarajevo already on the 10th of April. Do you know what happened to the hotels in Sarajevo proper, both -- and to the Serbs working in those hotels? We heard what you said about the hotel at Ilidza, that they were taken to the centre of town for their security. Now, down what happened to the hotels in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I witnessed a battle outside the hotel, the Bristol Hotel, the day the barricades went up, and I know what happen outside the hotel or in the confines of the hotel that I stayed in. Those are the two incidents in which I personally witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the Green Berets took control of all the hotels and forcefully evicted all the directors and Serb employees? We had a document showing that. We presented it with another witness. Do you know that that's what happened when you were there?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have anyone in town? You had 50, 60 people in town, did you not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had 56 or approximately 56 people when I was head of the monitor mission. When I went back to Sarajevo on the 10th of April, I was on my own in a different capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But from your diary we can see that you were in town frequently. You had meetings in town. So how is it possible that you didn't know what was going on in town, whereas you knew what was going on in Zvornik and Foca?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, Mr. Karadzic, I don't give you the opportunity of making accusations against me of being biased. Therefore, I will stick exactly to the truth, and I will say exactly where I was and what I did. And that's what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender that now, please. And may we have the directive back, 1600 was its number. This is my letter to Cutileiro, and there's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there will be no objection. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 05875 will be Exhibit D234.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you focus on the document from August 1992, that is to say, before the London Conference, during Carrington's time; you were still an associate of his. And this is what General Mladic writes. It's one of the directives. Number 3. I'd like to focus on item 3. No, number 1. "The enemy started violating the agreed 14-day cease-fire before its end, and offensive operations, in particular, have been underway since an agreement was reached between Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic on joint operations aimed at crushing the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and subjugating and exterminating the Serbian people." Not to read the whole paragraph, the beginning of paragraph 3 goes: "The objective of the planned operation is to break the blockade of Sarajevo by a concentrated attack by part of the forces on a suitable axes while simultaneously utilising part of the forces from," et cetera. "The enemy has settled scores mercilessly with the Serbian people and captured members of the SR BH army who were skilled with brutal and savage torture unrecorded in history." Now, Colonel, do you know that on the 3rd of June the Muslim forces in the village of Cemerno slaughtered these civilians in a very brutal way. They resorted to mutilation of Serb civilians. It was a very drastic event. Do you know about is it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's continue. "Certain European countries are doing their utmost during their influence in the Security Council and the EC to legalise the arming of Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and prevent the implementation of United Nations sanctions against Croatia because of the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina." Did you know that the regular units of the Croatian Army were constantly present in certain parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that certain elements of Croats wearing Croatian Army uniforms were periodically in the territory of Western Herzegovina, and I've already mentioned that in my testimony. Beyond that, I have no knowledge in relation to this directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's be very precise, Colonel. Were they elements of an entire brigade, or were they tactical units? Were they the elements of the whole brigade, the 108th Brigade of the Croatian Army, the Guards Brigade, and other brigades - and we'll show proof and evidence of that - but are they those elements, or is it an army?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have no idea whether they were elements. When we say "elements," it might seem that these are some tourists coming to wage war in Bosnia over the weekend. I'm talking about brigades, up to 50.000 Croat soldiers present in Bosnia. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge as to how many Croatia soldiers were in the territory of Bosnia. I know that some were. I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you do anything about this matter or did the conference do anything about this? Was Croatia threatened with sanctions or was it threatened with bombing or anything that would have been done had the Army of Serbia been present in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have certainly no comment on that suffice to say, Mr. Karadzic, you were seeing a document that you have in your possession of a report I made out on the situation of the Croatian soldiers in Bosnia. Beyond that, I have nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now go back to the directive. Last paragraph: "Some of these countries, Germany, Austria --" actually, can we look at page 3 in the English. "Just like some countries of the Islamic Community who are financing the Islamic jihad want to equip Muslim units so that they would be superior enough in strength to deal with the Army of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can now move to the third page in English and also the second page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The international community did not undertake specific measures that would treat equally all the forces in the conflict, but there is the influence of the major powers supporting the blockade of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, threatening the Serbian people of aggression, and threatening with armed intervention while the Croatian peoples are being declared the victims of aggression and tacit approval is given to their shipments of weapons through Austria and Croatia?" 20

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- actually, I think this is page 2 in the English. Perhaps we can go back to page 2 in the English so that all the parties could actually follow what I'm reading. This is paragraph 2:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The international community has not taken any peace steps. The so-called peace conference of BH and London under the leadership of Lord Carrington have not produced the desired results, and the conclusion can be drawn that their objective was to buy time for the consolidation of Croatian and Muslim forces in order to settle their score with the Serbian people?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And let's continue. It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, instead of reading out all the documents, put your question. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I have to back and look for page 5 to show what Mladic ordered. Can we look at page 5 in the Serbian, please, and also 5 in English, please. Before that, it is said, I have decided who will do what, and then he talks about the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are waiting to see the text on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 5, please. This is page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see it in the Serbian. In the English it's not so important. 5.4: "The Sarajevo Romanija Corps with persistent and active defence by main forces keep the positions reached in Sarajevo and the broader area and with part of the forces coordinate operations with the Hercegovina Corps in opening the Sarajevo-Trnovo-Kalinovik and Visegrad-Ustipraca-Gorazde road. And then it says: "Task," last sentence, "with persistent and active defence and gradually tighten the siege of Sarajevo and prevent the penetration towards Sarajevo." So the encirclement -- or, actually, that's the word. It's not "siege." It has been wrongly translated here. Colonel, do you see that in this article 5 -- actually, paragraph 4, Mladic insists on the opening of the road through Herzegovina? And we also see from the previous directive that the task or the objective of that is to have a way to deliver humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says in the -- that's what it says in the document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please tender directive number 3. Actually, this is already a Prosecution number. I don't know if it's already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree with the -- Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, with the accused's observation that that word - I don't know what it is - but it's wrongly translated as "siege"? It should have been translated as "encirclement"? I hope there's a way we can sort it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's rather a matter for the CLSS to decide what's the correct word. This document has not been, so far, admitted, but there's no objection to doing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D235, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, is that -- as I under it, all that you're saying is that, as all of us, you're reading the document and confirming that what is in the document is in the document. You're not confirming that you had a personal knowledge or that you were aware of the -- the opinions or the objectives of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's perfectly correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, we now have to go back to the transcript of your examination-in-chief so that we could be more specific about things. I'm afraid that there have been things that were said easily and imprecisely, and they can reflect very negatively on the Defence. I'm not accusing you of doing that deliberately, until I give you an opportunity to maybe be a little more specific.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to look at page 67 of the 21st of May now, please, so that we can look at that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it to you. This is a summary by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, and she says: He recalls that the local Serbs -- [In English] Serb leaders were often referred back to historical events and atrocities of the Second World War and expressed fears of their repetition." [Interpretation] Colonel, did you believe that we shouldn't be doing that, that we didn't have any grounds or reason to recall what was happening to us during World War II?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant here, Mr. Karadzic, is that on very many meetings that I had with various political parties there was the tendency for a lot of emphasis to be put on the atrocities in the Second World War. This was from all sides. I'm not accusing this of being only the Serbs. And I found that it wasn't helpful to use up a lot of valuable time in referring back constantly to what happened in the Second World War. So it became my practice to request the parties not to give me a history lecture any time I entered into negotiations or discussions. I felt it wasn't going to make any contribution towards understanding the current situation. And I felt it would be more important to talk about the concerns and the fears and the views and the opinions that the various parties had at the time that I was there. So I simply referred and asked the parties to please refrain from giving me a history lecture, because it seemed to be the tendency in that part of the world of referring constantly back to events of the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we be a little bit more specific. Now, you didn't say that Serbs talked about it constantly; you said the sides, the parties did. But here in the transcript it states that only the Serbs constantly referred back; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that, yes, I will acknowledge that. It was predominantly Serbs, but it was also Croats. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are talking about page 2646, and the witness did not say "only Serbs." He only refers to local Serbs, what they told him, but he doesn't say "only Serbs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you know -- do you agree with my assertion that there was no war in the Yugoslav territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina without having a fratricidal component, a component of civil war? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that we had reason for concern because Mr. Izetbegovic wore a Nazi uniform during World War II and was a friend of -- Hitler's friend, the great Mufti of Jerusalem, al-Husseini, and he hosted him in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you, Colonel, sir, that Mr. Izetbegovic, as an extremely developed intellectual person, from 1991 until his death he continuously developed the kind of thought regarding Islamic ideas, and because of that this could not be something that was far from our minds once he came into power in 1994, and because of that do you believe that we were not right to be concerned about that when he came to power? Mr. Izetbegovic was a member of the Young Muslims Organisation from 1939, and he never changed these beliefs. So I'm correcting the -- the year in the transcript. He never changed those beliefs from then until the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, where's the question in that? What you've done is made a statement of what you believe to be the factual situation. The proper way that that should come into the proceedings is, if and when you elect to give evidence, that you can explain your views and the historical basis for them, but I doubt very much whether Colonel Doyle is an expert on Mr. Izetbegovic and his intellectual and philosophical views as to Islam. If I'm wrong, Colonel Doyle will no doubt direct me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I agree with you, Your Honour. I'm aware that the ideological principles of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Izetbegovic would be different because they are from different ethnic groups. That's to be understood. But beyond that, I don't have a view as to what Mr. Izetbegovic might have been thinking or what was the basis of his philosophy. No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. There was a question, but it did not enter the transcript. My question is -- and then I will go back to what you said:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: As far as we're concerned, is that a remote distant past which should not have been mentioned once a person came to power who had worn a Nazi uniform during the war and socialised with Hitler's closest associates in the Middle East? Was that something that should not have been taken into account, this historical aspect as far as the Serbs were concerned, or was it something that had become a part of our present?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, history always has a tendency of becoming part of the presence, Mr. Karadzic, but I wasn't aware of these allegations against Mr. Izetbegovic. I was aware of his general background of being a Muslim and having different philosophies to you, and if that was some concern for you in the current situation, then I can understand that, but I have no basis for thinking that this was a strong influence on his current thinking. I simply don't know, and I don't have a view on it beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, you were in Sarajevo in the fall of 1991. Do you recall I made a public appeal to Mr. Izetbegovic to give up his Islamic Declaration so that tensions could be relieved and lessened, and he refused to do that? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic, I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this programme called the Islamic Declaration?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard reference to it, but I have no knowledge of it in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Izetbegovic, in 1947, was brought to trial because he continued the activities of young Muslims illegally, and in 1983 he was brought to trial because of the Islamic Declaration as a programme for the forceful change of the regime in Bosnia and in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that he was brought to trial in 1983, but nothing about 1947.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to the differences between me and Izetbegovic, stemming from the fact that we originate from two different communities. Do you know that Adil Zulfikarpasic is also a member of the Muslim ethnic community as well as Muhamed Filipovic and that they are very committed Muslims? Do you know that they are Muslims as well?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. I don't know these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Both of them are leaders of a smaller Muslim party, a Muslim-Bosniak organisation, and do you know that we, with that party, with the agreement of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness said he didn't know the two Muslims you referred to, there's no point on your part to continue that question. What is your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know or -- well, do you know Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that we agreed with Abdic and that we signed a truce sometime in 1993 with him?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I wasn't in Bosnia in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Mr. Abdic won the most votes from the Muslim people and that he wasn't considered a fundamentalist, labelled a fundamentalist, and that is to be respected, that the Muslim people voted for a man who wasn't a fundamentalist.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept now, Colonel, since I have informed you about this, so you do know now, that we had a historical Serbian-Muslim agreement and -- with Abdic who was from the SDA, that we concluded a truce and adhered to that? So do you accept that the difference between myself and Mr. Izetbegovic is not merely from our affiliation to the Serbian or Muslim corpus but that it is something deeper?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, Mr. Karadzic. I don't have a problem with that. What I'm saying to you is that I'm not aware of these points that you are raising and therefore don't wish to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you're behaving as if you do know. And you say that the differences stem from the fact that he's a Muslim and I'm a Serb, whereas I am telling you that there were Muslim parties with which we agreed with and got on well with. And I'm saying that it's because Mr. Izetbegovic was a fundamentalist, whereas these other Muslims were not. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I accept what you're saying. The dilemma I had was that most of the political parties in Bosnia were established along ethnic and religious lines, and that made the dilemma of getting them to a common agreement far more difficult to achieve. The various elements of whatever type of Muslims was not something that was of a major concern to me. I was dealing with members of the Presidency. As far as I was concerned, there were two members who were Serbs, there were two who were Muslims, and there were two who were Croats, and I think there was one other. So to me I wasn't concentrating in any way in the degrees of whether one was a fundamentalist Muslim or whether one was a different type of Muslim. No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Unfortunately, we did have to deal with that kind of thing, and this third person was Ejup Ganic, also a Muslim extremist. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say he was an extremist, that's fine. I don't think he was an extremist, but that's my opinion, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But he represented those others, the Jews, the Czechs, the Italians, all those minorities living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He represented them; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't a strict member of the SDA, the SDS, or the HDZ, and my understanding was that he was -- well, what you just referred to, as a Bosniak. In other words, somebody who didn't have a strong affiliation to any one side, and I accepted that. If you say he was representing the Jews and all the other non-main parties, I don't have a -- I don't have a comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Colonel, he couldn't be a Bosniak because that was for other ethnicities, for minorities. That was that place. And so we nominated a Jew for that post. Now, the SDA wanted to camouflage Ganic and make him a Yugoslav to have three members in the Presidency. Are you aware of the fact that it wasn't following the party line? It couldn't have been a Serb, a Croat, or a Bosniak, whereas he was. So was that trickery? Was that intended to dupe and deceive?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I have no idea. If you say this was trickery, that's your opinion. It isn't mine. So there we stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, Colonel, but I have to fight against many of your statements that you made in passing which are not precise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have a prosecution exhibit. 09446 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when we go through your transcript, we'll be able to have a look and see what that is like in documents, on the basis of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, this was admitted as Exhibit P925.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 10th of April, Colonel, 1992, 10th of April, 1992, and it's still the JNA there, the command of the 2nd Military District, the operative duty team, et cetera. Now let's see what they say about the enemy. Second sentence: "Under the guise of demobilisation of Croatian Army units, members of the HV who are from BH are being sent to BH in an organised manner, and conscripts are being mobilised in Croatia to replace them. Heavy weaponry is being brought in to the area of Bosanski Brod from Croatia intensively. The Croatian leadership is preoccupied with a situation in BH and hopes for large-scale armed conflicts as soon as possible. The enemy forces in the Kupres sector have been defeated at the Kupres-Vrata pass;" et cetera. Now, did you know of this large scale operation launched by the regular Croatian Army in the area of Kupres?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of action that had taken place in Kupres which involved members of the Croatian Army. The exact size, I wasn't. I'm just wondering, Mr. Karadzic, in that document, what does the enemy -- who does "the enemy" refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the Yugoslav People's Army refers to the Croatian Army as the enemy, and later on you will see that they were the paramilitaries, too, that were the enemy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we move on to page 3 -- or, rather, page 2 in the English. And I think it's page 2 in the Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll read it out in Serbian: "The situation in the territory --" [No interpretation] "[In English] The situation in the 2nd "Vojna Oblast," military zone of responsibility, is becoming increasingly troubled and is reaching boiling point. The situation is deteriorating in trouble spots, especially in Visegrad, Zvornik, Jajce, and Sarajevo sector."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "[In English] Hatred of the JNA among the Muslims and Croatian population is becoming even greater. The president of B and H claims that the JNA is the only force capable of acting to save the Muslim population in the Zvornik sector but is unwilling to do so, which will only compound further the hostile stance of the Muslim population toward the JNA." [Interpretation] Then the next page. "[In English] Armed conflict between the Sarajevo Romanija -- Romanija SAO and Green Berets and the MUP of Ministry of Interior continues throughout the day with occasional pauses with the use of small-arms fire and mortars. Mortar fire was again used today, directed at feature -- at -- in the city of Sarajevo. The armed formations of Green Berets, armed citizens, and MUP members control all movement in the city of Sarajevo and all the roads in the corps zone." [Interpretation] So here this intelligence officer is informing that the Muslim part of the MUP, the Green Berets, and the armed civilians took over control of the city of Sarajevo. Is that what you knew too?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information at that time was that certain areas of the city were under control by the various parties and that there was continuous harassment and attacks. The exact detail of what occurred, I simply don't know. This refers to a report on the 10th of April. The 10th of April is the day I returned to Bosnia, having been away for some weeks back in Ireland. But I'm aware generally that there was quite a considerable amount of conflict going on. Movement in the city was very difficult, so I wasn't in a position at that stage to be able to get detailed information as to who was doing what. And I had met with the commander of the second group, but he certainly didn't give me the detail that is in this document when I met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now under the title "5th Corps," third sentence: "The arming of the SDA [In English] party and the HDZ. Paramilitary formations is being legalised under the guise of the newly established Territorial Defence. "In the Banja Luka garrison, acts of sabotage in the town and attacks against Islamic and Catholic places of worship are on the increase which may cause the situation to escalate even further." [Interpretation] Do you see, Colonel, that this intelligence officer of the Yugoslav People's Army is painting the right picture and stating that it was uncontrolled elements who were responsible for doing all this?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly in reference to his report from Banja Luka saying that the sabotage at the time and the attacks against Islamic and Catholic places are on the increase certainly would indicate that the JNA were painting a picture from all sides. These acts of sabotage in the town and attacks, I don't know who these were committed by against the places of worship. So, I mean, have you a specific question for me on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what I want to ask you, Colonel, is this: Do you see that the Yugoslav People's Army is monitoring the situation, not taking part, and that the assessment was -- that it made, was that there was an uncontrolled eruption, and we'll see that on the penultimate page, conclusions and forecasts. And I'll come to my question after I read this bit out. Or, rather, after you take a look at the penultimate page. The activities of the ECMM are there too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's L006-8130 in English. That's the page number. May we have page 130 of the English. Or, rather, it's number 7. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He says that Cutileiro has arrived at about 1500 hours. "[In English] On April the 10th in 1992, the Portuguese ambassador Mr. Cutileiro arrived in Sarajevo." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. And then down there conclusions and forecasts. "[In English] Uncontrolled eruption of fighting in B and H can be expected in the situation of widespread anarchy and lawlessness, and the units of the 2nd military district will -- will very probably be dragged into it. Large-scale provocation and attacks on JNA units, military installations, officers and their family members can be expected." [Interpretation] Now let's see how you characterise this. The question is this, Colonel: Do you see that the army is taking an objective and neutral stance with respect to the situation that it is assessing?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time in Sarajevo, I was quite satisfied that the JNA were not getting actively involved in the various -- in the various attacks that were taking place in the city of Sarajevo. I have no evidence or information as to what they might have been doing in other areas of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is already an exhibit, I believe; right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now may we take a look at page 68 of the transcript where your views are being interpreted by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Have we got that page? I'll read it out: "[In English] On March the 2nd, 1992, the day after the results of the referendum were announced, shooting commenced in Sarajevo, and barricades were elected by the Serbs. " And at the end it says that you said: "[In English] Colonel Doyle was informed by the person in charge at that time barricades would only be dismissed upon Karadzic's specific direction." [Interpretation] Do you agree that that's not what it says in your diary? And do you agree that the barricades were dismantled only after the agreement reached between Mr. Dukic and the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just need to check my diary here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just for orientation, we're talking about page 2647 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You already answered that, but I'd just like to -- well, we showed you that. Do you remember the agreement -- or, rather, the Presidency meeting of the 2nd of March?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the one in which there were demands. Are we talking about that? Okay. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's see what it says here. On the 10th of April, 1992, Martin Bell of the BBC informed Colonel Doyle [In English] That about 25.000 refugees were moving from Zvornik, [Interpretation] and so on. Now, you say that you were informed about ethnic cleansing. Now, who informed you of this ethnic cleansing, and how was that piece of information formulated precisely?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information was given to me by members of the ECMM. And So that's where I got the information. How it was compiled, I don't know. I wasn't a member of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it said that ethnic cleansing was being committed?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, yes, that people were being forcibly removed from their areas where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the phrasing. Were you told that ethnic cleansing was being committed?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We understood this to be ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that the term "ethnic cleansing" was introduced publicly much later, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't -- I don't have a comment on that. I would have to say now that after 18 years I don't have as good a recollection as I might have had at the time, but we were -- we were satisfied that there was a huge amount of displacement of residents from various locations generally along the east side of the country in places like Bijeljina and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the departure of a large number of Serbs from Livno even before the war, in late March and early April?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was actually going on in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no detailed knowledge of what was going on in Zvornik except on the basis of what I was informed by Mr. Bell of the BBC, and you will see there that I simply put down that 25.000 refugees were on the move. I don't know what direction they were going in, but they were leaving the town or the area of Zvornik. And that's the information I passed on to you. You asked me where I got the information from, and I told you I got it from Martin Bell of the BBC, and you said you did not believe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will have a break. This time we will have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you noted the address by Mr. Vojo Kupresanin and one part of his speech in the Assembly cited here. First of all, do you know that Vojo Kupresanin was the president of a small party that was in coalition with us, the homeland front, and that he was not a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. I don't know this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But on page 75, the question was -- just to say, it's Mr. Kupresanin speaking. "[In English] This can be seen from the two pages previous, and he is saying," and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter number 39, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am not trying to disown Kupresanin, but I would just like you to know something a little bit more about him. He was not a member of the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5921. That document has already been admitted, I think. P921, P921. Prosecution document. And then page 53 of that document, please, which is quoted in the transcript. In the English, this is page 77. In the Serbian, it's page 53, and in the English it's page 77. The English text, that's not it; but in the Serbian, we are on the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the middle paragraph: "The generals and the Serb army --" I'm going to be reading in the Serbian because the translations are not good. I'm going to point that out. "The generals and the Serb army did not have adequate Serb leaders." Colonel, I'm reading what the Prosecution failed to present as a whole statement. "... they didn't have adequate Serbian leaders. Nobody told those Serb officers, Gentlemen, this and that is your task. After all, the Serbian Democratic Party was not preparing the Serbian people for war. We do remember that our leaders, and I'm not criticising here but only try to point out the mistakes we made, thinking of the leaders, said that there would be no war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that we would politically solve the problems. That is exactly the same thing that is going on in Geneva, and they have been pulling our leg for years. So the head of a small party which was in the coalition with us is pointing out that the Serbian Democratic Party did not adequately prepare the people for war." And now the next paragraph, we have it in the transcript partially from line 12 on page 75, and it says: "Now we're going back to this. We had aviation, howitzers, tanks, cannon, but what did the Muslims have? A gun here and there, a machine-gun that they had bought from the Serbs," and so on and so forth. First of all, sir, Colonel, we have the tense wrongly translated here. It says "we have," and in the Serbian, in the original, it says "we had had," and so I would like to indicate, Colonel, that this is an important matter. Secondly, Mr. Kupresanin is speaking about Yugoslavia and the army, which was actually not told what it was supposed to do in Yugoslavia, not about Republika Srpska. Do you see the difference here, now that you are able to see both of these paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, you seem to be rather selective in the portions of this document that you -- you are referring to. I've seen the sentence which talks about possession of the aviation and the howitzers and the tanks --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that, Colonel. I put a question to you, so please answer the question and don't go beyond the -- what is being asked. And don't work for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic. That's not a proper comment on your part. Don't interrupt the witness when he answers your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, he's not answering my question. And this is something that can be put in the re-examination by the Prosecution. Now, I see that the witness is completely biased. He's answering questions that I didn't actually put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your interference is unacceptable --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to show the Serbs in a worse light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would ask Dr. Karadzic to ask the direct question again because he has said so much in the last few minutes that I don't know how many question he wants me to answer. So if you would ask me a question, Mr. Karadzic, I will attempt to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you remember I told you some time ago, if you ask broad open-ended questions you get broad open-ended answers. If you closed, direct questions and concentrate the witness's mind on a single issue, you are much more likely to get a single, concise answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: The Prosecution interpreted only this bottom paragraph for us. The previous passage speaks about how the Serbian Democratic Party did not prepare the people for war, and that is being said by a leader of a different party that -- and that he's taking issue with that. Do you see that here, please?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I'm reading here is that the generals and the Serb army did not adequate Serb -- did not have adequate Serb leaders. So I -- I really don't understand what is being said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Continue: "Finally, the Serbian Democratic Party did not prepare the Serbian people for war." Do you see that written there?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And, Mr. Karadzic, I can see it, but I'm trying to understand exactly what that's supposed to mean. The Serb Democratic Party was not preparing Serb people for the war. What -- I'd like to have the context for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The context, Colonel, is this: In the transcript it is presented as if Mr. Kupresanin is saying that at that point in time we had planes, howitzers, tanks, cannon, and so on and so forth. What I'm actually telling you now is that this is something that was in the past, that we had had, thinking of the Yugoslavia, which should have been preserved. Now I am giving you two paragraphs for your consideration instead of one that the Prosecution opted for. Do you see that this previous paragraph explains better this subsequent paragraph that is cited in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I'm getting from this, Mr. Karadzic, is that you're not happy that there's an exact accurate translation of the document that is in your language to the English language. So I'm not too sure what I should be referring to. Am I referring to what you believe the English translation should be or what exactly the translation is on the document? That's my dilemma at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what I'm trying to point out here is that with the previous paragraph, this paragraph is properly translated as "we had aviation," and it looks different than it looks in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't read Serbo-Croat, so what exactly do you wish me to say? The only document that I understand is the document that's in the English language in front of me, and are you saying that that's not an adequate translation of the original document? I'm sorry, I think you will have to explain it to me because I really don't understand what we're getting at here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the document that's translated before us says: "We had aviation," in past tense.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the transcript it is not cited correctly by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. It says here "we have aviation."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, Colonel, do you agree that this is a major difference? At this point in time we "have" in January 1993 or we "had." Is this a significant difference or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there are two different documents with two different translations that are different, then, of course, there are differences. But I'm looking at a document in front of me which simply says "we had aviation, howitzers, tanks, and cannons." Now, if you're telling me there's another document which says "we have aviation, howitzers, tanks, and cannons," then, of course, it's different. But I don't know what the official translation is at this stage because you are -- what you're saying is the translation isn't accurate. So I'm not too sure what I would be looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I'm looking -- I'm reading the transcript of 21st of May, the last line, line 25 of 2654. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff is cited as correctly citing: "We had aviation, howitzers, tanks." If you have the transcript which says "we have," it's a typo. I don't know how come you have that translation. And the correct one should be the document we have in the e-court, in our exhibit, and our transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a transcript where it says on page 75, line 12, "We have aviation, howitzers, tanks," and so on. This is the translation that I have -- actually, the transcript that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I told you before, the transcript is being edited by a court reporter, correcting all the typos, et cetera, so the official -- you have to check what the official transcript would look like.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I assume that Dr. Karadzic is looking at LiveNote, but LiveNote, of course, always has a lot of mistakes in it. But what we get in -- a few hours after the session is the correct version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the corrected LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then this has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, does the leader of a smaller party here criticise the Serbian Democratic Party for opting for a political solution and for not preparing the people for war?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would appear to be what's inferred in this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now when it is said "we had aviation," you allow for the possibility that Mr. Kupresanin, who is the leader and the founder of a party called the Otadzminski Front [phoen], the Homeland Front, speaks about Yugoslavia, which had everything it needed to preserve the country, and not about Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I really don't know. I simply don't know, Mr. Karadzic. I'm getting confused now because we have a document in front us and you're indicating that it's not an accurate translation of an official document. So I don't know. What it says here is the generals in the Serb army did not have adequate Serb leaders. That's one point. Then they talk about the party was not preparing the Serb army for war. That's a second point. And then the third point relates to munitions and -- and tanks, et cetera. Now, you're saying if the official document that we are to accept actually says "we had aviation" as if that were to mean we had it in the past and we don't have it now, that could be an interpretation. That may be something which is the opinion of something. I simply don't know. And if that's the case then, this was an official transcript from the Assembly of the Republika Srpska, and maybe it should be more accurate to give a more definitive explanation as to what exactly it meant. But here I think we're talking about opinions. And I don't want to give my opinion on this because if I give you my opinion, I may be accused of being biased, and I don't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but the Prosecution used that in their interpretation of your meeting with Mr. Kupresanin whom you actually considered as more radical. So the Prosecution used this to corroborate your impression about Mr. Kupresanin. Mr. Kupresanin is a deputy. He has the right to say whatever he wants. And he cannot be held responsible for that. And the government and the Assembly is held responsible for the documents it issues. Resolutions, conclusions, and so on and so forth. So anyway, we have finished with this. Not only did he say what you mentioned, but he also said one more thing: Nobody told the Serb officers what their task was. That's what he said, and that is the objection by all the Yugoslavs, that the Yugoslav Army was not issued with the assignment of protecting Yugoslavia in accordance with its constitutional duties. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no comment to that because I simply don't know what directives were given to the Federal Army of Yugoslavia. I mean, how would I know that? I assume the JNA Army was an army for all of the republics, a federal army, and that it was doing its tasks. Exactly what those tax were individually, I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 82 of the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where you are cited as saying that: "The president of Bosnia-Herzegovina claims that the JNA's [In English] only force capable of acting to save the Muslim population is Zvornik sector but it is unwilling to do so which will only compound further the hostile stance of the Muslim population towards the JNA." [Interpretation] Let me just ask you briefly: Up until Zvornik, was the position of Izetbegovic and the Muslim political elite friendly towards the JNA or was it hostile right from the very beginning towards the Serbian side, the JNA? To simplify, when do the misunderstandings begin between the Muslim leadership and the JNA? Would you agree that this was at the point in time when they refused to send recruits and reservists to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that is one of the factors that may have contributed to it. The other factor, of course, is the first time - and I refer to this in my testimony - that I had a meeting with the prime minister in which he referred to the JNA as an army of occupation and that the JNA were taking in munitions from another republic under what could only be described as -- as covert means. So there was a general suspicion. You'll also be aware of the fact that it was my recommendation to the prime minister as head of the monitor mission that there was no reason why there should not have been dialogue between the Government of Bosnia and the federal army because they were a major force in the territory. And that was my recommendation. So I don't disagree with the points that you're raising there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to add that Mr. Pelivan was defending the interests of Croatia, and he was a Croat, and not the interests of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was not an official B and H government decision. You didn't have a government decision. This was actually an opinion of Mr. Pelivan at that point in time when you had your meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've adequately explained that yesterday, so I'm not going to repeat it, Mr. Karadzic.
