utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The question is not in the transcript. I asked: "Is that so?"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has this transcript been admitted in its entirety from the session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 1D01260.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, Colonel, this is a report by General Kukanjac of the 5th of May after what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same document is a 65 ter document, 3721. That's a Prosecution document. And there is an English version as well. So perhaps it would be better to look at that, 3721. This is of May 7th, after the massacre in Dobrovoljacka Street, and he's writing -- the command of the 4th Corps writes to the commander personally, and this is a very interesting and important document. Can we now look at page 2 in the Serbian, and then this is page 8A in the English. Sorry. This is page 2, but it's paragraph marked with the number 8. I think it's actually the same in the English and the B/C/S. Page two, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it says, under (A): "Based on the experience gained in Slovenia, Croatia, and Macedonia, the district command made a timely assessment that the soldiers of the army are facing a difficult time and that we have to start evacuating to safe areas in which connection the following was carried out: "For months, weapons, ammunition, mines and explosives, and other equipment are being relocated to safe areas with long-term potential for the army." Colonel, sir, do you agree that the army should not remain in an encirclement where it is considered to be an enemy side or entity?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if this is based on the attack on the convoy on the 2nd of March, I can well understand the comments of the military commander putting this down in writing. I can certainly understand that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to draw your attention to where they are relocating their equipment. "To safe areas with long-term potential for the army," it says. Now, Colonel, are they moving the weapons for the Serbs to Serb territory or for themselves?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to this report, they are moving weapons, ammunition, mines and explosives to safe areas so that they can be used by the army at a future date. That's my interpretation of that -- first point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this document already an exhibit? It's a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We did not admit this over the agreement on the part of the Prosecution, but given the answer offered by the witness right now, we are minded to admit it this time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit Number D236.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, on page 84 there was a question from Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. She said: "Colonel, you testified that you spoke about information on ethnic cleansing in Foca. With Mr. Koljevic in April 1992. [In English] The term ethnic cleansing, what did you understand it to entail?" [Interpretation] You say what you understand the term to mean, and I say that the term ethnic cleansing came into use later on. But let me ask you, How did you know what was going on in Foca?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference I made to Foca was simply that the monitor mission was attempting to go to Foca because of certain information it received. I don't know what that information was, and I was aware that when they came back, after failing to get to Foca, and I asked them, Why is it you didn't get to Foca? They told me that they were stopped by the JNA who told them that they could not guarantee their safety and security. And I a general discussion with Mr. Koljevic who approached me about that, and Mr. Koljevic regretted that we weren't able to get there, that's what he said to me, and that he would try to see -- could he arrange passage to Foca, which subsequently did not occur. That's the only reference I have to Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I remember that, Colonel, and I know that Mr. Jeremy Brade was with Koljevic and that there was still snow on the ground and that Mr. Koljevic was threatened by the local territorials because he failed to protect the people, as they said, and that he was threatened by execution. Did Mr. Brade inform you of that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. I'm not too sure why you're mentioning Mr. Brade, because I don't have a recollection of -- of Mr. Brade at that time. So you might have to remind me, but I just don't recall that. Not the element to do with Mr. Brade, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was an attempt to break through to Koljevic and Brade in April, and both of them informed me that the people were furious over there, having been left without protection and that they threatened Vice-President Koljevic, although they liked him, but they threatened him because they considered him to be responsible as a person in authority. But, right, you say you don't remember that. So I just told you about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D77 next, please. Or, rather, 00077. 1D77.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, Colonel, I'm going to show you a document from the Muslim intelligence service about the circumstances and situation in Foca, and I want to ask you, Did you know that Halid Cengic, the father of Hasan Cengic, formed the first Muslim paramilitary formation during the days of the Communists, before the elections in 1990 in Foca?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's take a look at this document from the Muslim intelligence -- Military Intelligence Service. That's the first page, the cover page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we turn to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And towards the end it says "namely," the paragraph starting with "namely." "Namely, after the democratic elections, Taib Lojo, an electrical engineer, respectable citizen of the vice-president of the Foca SDA, was appointed president of the Foca SO. However, from the very beginning, Senad Sahinpasic, also known as Saja, and Halid Cengic, who are related, have had the greatest political influence in the SDA, thanks to the powerful support of influential relatives and friends from Sarajevo, especially Muhamed Cengic, the then deputy prime minister ..." Now, do you know of a journal by the name of "Vox," owned by this same man, Senad Sahinpasic, who was a deputy in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be an error in the transcript. The journal "Vox" was owned by Sahinpasic. It was a journal, a magazine. Now we'll see what it wrote about, that journal. Magazine, magazine. "Casopis" as in "magazine."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now let's continue. Sahinpasic is a private trader from Foca and a deputy in the citizens' Assembly of BiH. And Cengic is an accountant at the Mljin [phoen], a work organisation in Uskopljina, and councillor in the Foca SO. Now, let's move further down. "From the time they came into power, having gathered around them their family and friends, they started with all kinds of fraud and smuggling which brought them huge amounts of money. The increasingly complex political situation and deteriorating interethnic relations during 1991 played into their hands since arms smuggling was flourishing. And they did nothing to appease the situation, but on the contrary, incite it with their actions and political activity. "They included Aziz Sljivo and a wide circle of men loyal to them in the armed smuggling so that the Muslim people in this area from fear of the ever-increasing Chetnik threat are giving their last penny to those whom they have elected to protect their interest to supply them with weapons. So they pay, the rifles that Sahinpasic and Cengic sell them, for from 1.200 to 1.500 German marks. According to some intelligence, 5.200 rifles came to Foca via the SDA, which Sahinpasic and Cengic sold." Now, did you know that the SDA of Foca was armed in this way before the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that. As I said, attempts to get to Foca failed, so I have no information from it. And I notice this report was made out in July, I think, 1993. I saw from the front. Even though it refers to something in 1992. So, in other words, this document was made out a year after I had left Bosnia. So I'm not familiar with it or the people that are being mentioned in it or the -- the contents of what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, what I want to say is the following: It was known to us, and it was known to the Serbs in Foca as well, and the conflict broke out because the SDA had 5.200 rifles and units, while the Serb side was waiting for the JNA to protect it. And that is why they threatened Professor Koljevic, because the JNA did not reach Foca in time to protect them. So are you aware of the fact that the JNA was late in coming to Foca?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge of this, Mr. Karadzic, and as I said, if -- if the JNA had given an escort to the team to go in, maybe events would have been different, but they didn't, and they didn't go in, so we'd no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you see now why the JNA was not able to guarantee security? Do you see that it was because of these 5.200 rifles that the JNA was not certain that it could guarantee its own safety, let alone the safety of a foreign delegation?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, if what is said in this report is true, then that may well have been the case. But I don't know. I mean, this is just another document. How true it is, I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have the last page of this document so that we can see that it was signed by the chief of the military security administration, General Fikret Muslimovic, who was a Muslim and that there's no room for doubt. He is informing his command about the situation in Foca from before the war to the present day, that is to say, until 1993. Here we have the original seal and signature of Fikret Muslimovic. But since it's 1993, I won't pursue the subject, but we can see that they are describing 1991 and 1992. May I tender this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. The witness couldn't confirm anything about the content. Pursuant to our consistent rule, we will not admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But then I have to ask the Colonel whether he stands by his assertion about the events in Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I don't recall the Colonel making any stand about events in Foca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What events --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on page 84. I just quoted it all. On page 84 of what I have. The question was:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you testified that you spoke about information on [In English] ethnic cleansing in Foca with Mr. Koljevic in April 1992. The term ethnic cleansing and so on. [Interpretation] And then the Colonel answers: "Well, my interpretation of the term ethnic cleansing was ..." and so on and so on. So its linked to Foca. It is linked and refers to Foca.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already mentioned, Mr. Karadzic, the only reference to Foca that occurred at that time, and it was information I received from the monitor mission. Exactly what happened and who did what, I simply don't know. The reference was made to the term ethnic cleansing, or I thought it was. Certainly a forced removal of a population. And the monitor mission was not in a position of going to Foca in order to check it out because the JNA stopped them and said they couldn't go forward. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did the JNA prevent them, or could they not guarantee their safety?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA physically prevented them, and the excuse for preventing them was they said, We cannot guarantee your safety and your security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that that was an excuse?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm simply letting you know what I was informed of by a team of the monitor mission. I have absolutely no reason to disbelieve what they said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Brade informed me quite differently of the situation. Do you, Colonel, maintain that in Foca there was not any heavy fighting going on before the Serbs left and went to one area of Foca and the Muslims to the other? Did this happen without fighting or was it because of the fighting and after the fighting?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, Mr. Karadzic. The monitor mission did not get into Foca, and I don't want to make any comment on what you might feel is speculation on my part. So I'm not going to say anything more on something I don't know personally about. As to what Mr. Brade may have said, I -- I have no idea what you're talking about there. Mr. Brade may have said to Mr. Koljevic what you think he said or he did say it. I simply don't know. I can't verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you don't have reliable information to the effect that there was any ethnic cleansing in Foca; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said it was any reliable information, Mr. Karadzic. I simply said what the monitor mission told me. I've said that on a few occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 85 you say that you don't remember -- or, rather, when I questioned you, you said you don't remember the letter sent to you by Prime Minister Djeric, and you said that you kept the letters -- you kept your letters, but you didn't keep that particular letter. So may we ask you now to hand over your correspondence, the correspondence you had during the war and that you kept and everything related to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not too sure what you're getting at here, Mr. Karadzic. All of my documents I handed in to the Tribunal when I made my witness statement in 1990 -- 1995 or 1996 - I can't remember. So beyond that, I'm not too sure what -- what you're seeking. I certainly -- I certainly have absolutely no recollection of receiving any letter from Mr. Djerkic [sic]. The name is not familiar with me. And I suggested yesterday, if that letter was sent in English, I certainly would have reacted to the content of that letter had I received it in English because its content is directly different to my interpretation of what happened up in Pale. So there would have been no reason for me not to have taken action on that, had I received it. I have no recollection of receiving it. I have no record of receiving it. I have no knowledge of what it says. What I have done is I have commented on the content of that letter which I totally disagree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you explained that, you said that you kept your letters but that you don't have that letter amongst your collection.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You may have misinterpreted me. I haven't -- I haven't possession of any letters of this nature that I haven't -- or reports that I haven't handed in to the Tribunal. So maybe -- maybe I -- I said it incorrectly. If I did, I do apologise. I don't have any letters of a personal issue that -- that I haven't handed up and that refer to my service in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, possibly you said "recollection," whereas the interpretation I got or I heard "collection," so that is also possible. Now, on page 86, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff says -- we now go down to paragraph 5, and I'll read to you. It says -- and that's from a report by Mr. Goulding: "All international observers agree [In English] that what is happening is a concerted effort by the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the acquiescence and at least some support from the JNA to create ethnically pure regions in the context of negotiations on the cantonisation of the republic in the EC conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina and chaired by Ambassador Cutileiro. And the techniques used of the seizure of territory by military force," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] Who informed Mr. Goulding in this way?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I would assume it was the United Nations force that was operationally deployed in Bosnia, and maybe a certain amount of the United Nations observers who were deployed in different parts of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you say which territories did the Serbs take or occupy that was not already theirs?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not able to say that, Mr. Karadzic, but I certainly was aware at the time, that there was -- there was assertions by Serbs that they were the original occupiers of certain territories and that's the reason why they were taking them. I have no exact detail of that. It was just a general view that people of all races and all ethnic backgrounds were being expelled from certain territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because of the information that I received when I was head of the mission by the monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was information from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You say that in one place, don't you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then, of course, I received a lot of information from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina because I had frequent meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You think that that information should have been checked that, it could have been one-sided?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information would have been better checked if we had been guaranteed and continued to enjoy the freedom of movement that was part of the condition under which the monitor mission was deployed. The monitor mission was an unarmed observer group of monitors who were deployed into the territory with the agreement of all sides. And the conditions under which they were deployed was that they were to be given freedom of movement and safety and security. The monitor mission was withdrawn from the territory of Bosnia on the morning of the 11th of May, which was 24 hours before I left, I think, because that guarantee of freedom of movement and safety and security could not be guaranteed. That left the monitor mission in a predicament of wondering why they couldn't have been given these guarantees any more and the questions as to whether there were events taking place that people didn't want them to become aware of. That's what I assume. The United Nations, on the other hand, stayed deployed in Bosnia. So maybe they're in a better position to give you some idea, better than -- than myself or the monitor mission. And as I mentioned, the UNPROFOR also had in its -- in its ranks a group of monitors that were -- a group of observers that were deployed in the early days who were based in different parts of the republic. So maybe some of those personnel are in a better position to answer your queries in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware, Colonel, that we were in favour of a greater presence of Asian and African elements that we believed were impartial and that we distrusted representatives of the West, especially those from NATO countries, and that is why we asked for more Asian and African troops and observers? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no idea to that. I had no hand, act, or part in the deployment or selection of observers for the United Nations. As you know, I wasn't a member of the United Nations, so I have no idea. I know that the original United Nations observers that were deployed into Bosnia were volunteers of those nations that were already in service in other UN missions. The first UN people to go into Bosnia were officers from existings -- existing United Nations missions throughout the world. But, no, I'm not aware of your point in relation to Asian and African elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, the mission of the European Community actually ignored Serbs to quite an extent. They avoided being photographed, being photographed with them out of fear that that would be understood as some kind of recognition, although we were not actually asking for anything. So do you doubt that we considered Western countries' representatives as biased towards the Serbs? Of course, not you personally. We considered you to be quite impartial, but representatives from European countries.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the period that I was held of the monitor mission, there was no instance that was every brought to my attention that the European Community ignored Serbs or that they avoided being photographed. I never issued any directive as head of the mission to that extent, so I can't accept that. And I'm surprised you actually bring it up, because -- and I'm also quite surprised on the reference to Western countries, because I wasn't aware of it. As I've said before, the ECC mission that I was a member of was made welcome by all sides, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, by all political parties, and we attempted to do our job in an impartial manner, and we were never at any stage refused any meetings by any sides in the conflict. It was only when the military situation appeared to be escalating that the monitors were being stopped from going to areas. As I said, they were -- this was done by the JNA on the premises that they wanted to ensure that the monitors who were unarmed would have safety and security and freedom of movement, and this became more difficult to achieve and for some reason that I'm not directly aware of because I wasn't with the monitor mission at the time they were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I'm waiting for the interpretation. Can we look at D217 to see what General MacKenzie says about this, who was there at the same time. But let me remind you, Colonel, sir, you refused to go to a dinner in Ilidza so you won't be photographed with the Serbs and in Pale so that that would not be taken as recognition of Republika Srpska. We were not asking you to recognise Republika Srpska, but we were an acknowledged, recognised party in the negotiations and in the conflict, so you couldn't have been surprised. You were probably restrained in relation to the Serbian side, but -- but you believe the Presidency on its word.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd just like to correct you there, Mr. Karadzic. I did not refuse to go to the dinner in Ilidza. It was during the dinner when I listened to comments that I certainly didn't agree with that I decided that I would leave the dinner. So that's one correction. And as I mentioned before, the conditions under which I went to Pale that were agreed upon with not honoured by the Serbs of Pale on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that I officially said, when I was asked do I accept foreign troops, that I officially said to the mediators that we would be glad to see Asian and African troops for which we believed didn't have any interest in the matters and for whom we believed -- and who we believed would be impartial. Could you just answer with a yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I know that you officially asked for these? No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 182 now, please, of this book by General MacKenzie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 11th of May you were still there. I'm going to read it. We will have it. "[In English] The European Community had been conducting marathon peace talks over the previous few days."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 182, not 183. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "[In English] The EC continued to exclude the Bosnian Serbs from the deliberations and as a result was becoming less and less popular with them." Do you see that General MacKenzie had a good sense and is of the same opinion as myself?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that General MacKenzie has a different sense, not necessarily a good sense, because it was the same that you had, Mr. Karadzic. I've already explained why it is that we did not have the Bosnian Serbs at those talks. The Bosnian Serbs were invited, and they didn't want to come to the location because they had more or less left the city. They had established their headquarters in Pale. And just because they weren't at the talks doesn't mean that they weren't invited. They were invited. The second point on that is most of these talks were concentrating on the withdrawal of the federal army, the JNA, from the territory of Bosnia, and they came to the talks. And the third point is that General MacKenzie is a United Nations military officer. I was a monitor from the European Union doing a different task. He is entitled to his opinion, as I'm sure I am to mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, sir. I agree as to the opinions, but we're talking about criminal proceedings here now, and we need to stick to the facts. And the facts were that we were always available for all talks at the airport, in Lukavica, in Pale, and abroad, Brussels, London, Lisbon, and so on and so forth. Do you remember a single conference that we left early or did not attend?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at February 28th. You were with Hebib, high-ranking police official. I'm talking about your diary. This is D217. Can we put that away now? We don't need it. But in your diary of the 28th of February, you were with Hebib, and you were at the Presidency then, on the 2nd and the 3rd of March. On the 28th, you didn't see any Serbs. You did see Hebib. On the 2nd and the 3rd of March, you saw the Presidency. On the 5th of March, you saw the Presidency and met with Ganic. There are no Bosnian Serbs anywhere. On the 6th you were at the Presidency, and you met with Hebib, who is not a Presidency member, but you did see him. On the 7th you had dinner with Kukanjac and Aksentijevic from the army, but they are not Bosnian Serbs. On the 9th, Spanish monitors. On the 10th, the Presidency. There are no Serbs anywhere. On the 11th, Presidency. On the 12th, Konjicija and Prlic. And then here we have the 13th, there is nothing. The 14th, again, Hebib. Look, for half a month you had no connection with Bosnian Serbs, Colonel, and the conference was underway, and we were getting ready for the 18th of March to accept the Lisbon Agreement. 16th, the Presidency. On the 17th, Dr. Hadzic; he's also a Muslim. On the 18th there was an interview on television, and then on the 19th Ganic and the Presidency. So for almost a month you had no contacts with the Bosnian Serbs. Wasn't General MacKenzie right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not right. I made myself available to anybody in Bosnia that wanted to come and talk to me; all sides, all communities, all religions, all ethnic groups. There were some people who were more available than others. Any day I went to the Presidency, I was available to talk to members of the Presidency, any members of the Presidency; Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. If, Mr. Karadzic, you are trying to get the message across here that somehow I was trying to treat the Serbs any less than any other -- any of the other ethnic groups, I refute it strongly. And I will not have my integrity questioned in any way by those comments. I take it as a personal insult. I never ever refused to meet you or anybody else in the Bosnian Serb side. You can look at the diary all you want. People came to me. I went to people. I made myself available. There has never been an accusation against me or members of the monitor mission of the type that you're trying to make here, and I refute it vehemently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, please don't be insulted. I am speaking about official matters, not private matters. You were without contact with the Serbian side for a whole month. Should Professor Koljevic have asked to have been received by you or Mrs. Plavsic for you to be able to receive them and inform the European Community on Serb positions, or you should have perhaps asked for meetings with them. And if I am wrong, is your diary wrong, which indicates that there have been -- there were no contacts with the Serb side for a whole month? And is General MacKenzie right because he was saying the same thing that I am saying, that you were being -- that you were excluding us and that is why you were popular [as interpreted]. I mean, not you, but the European Monitor mission.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I've already said everything I'm going to say about this matter. I have no intention of repeating myself or changing any of it. You can take it or you can leave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we accept this diary with the redactions in which I state that the European Monitor mission does not have any insight into the state of affairs and the political efforts by the Serbian side? We were not in Pale then. It was March. We were in the middle of Sarajevo, so it was very easy to communicate with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No -- of course I object against his remarks that are just being made, but I have no objection against admitting this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Page 63, line 7 of the transcript, Dr. Karadzic says: "... and that is why you were less popular."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the 65 ter number of this diary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have to put it under seal? I take it that you voluntarily handed over the photocopy of it, redacting some confidential part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted as evidence as ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D238 [sic], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 65 ter 11086 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you briefly, Colonel. Is that my statement that I signed in Lisbon on the 27th of May, 1992? Do you remember that I asked our police to escort the convoys, that you didn't ask me to do that; I did that of my own accord?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're asking me about a statement, which I -- oh, hold on. Here. I'll have a look at it. Can I have a moment, please. Yes, that's the document that was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 2 does is say that the Serb police was prepared, although we didn't ask for that, was prepared to extend their full co-operation for regular escorts of humanitarian aid through Serbian-controlled territory to any destination and to members of any community to avoid any misunderstandings? Do you remember that, and do you remember that the proposal came from us? It was our proposal.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that it came from you, but I accept it fully. It's in the document which you signed, so I accept it. Whether it was actually put into practice or not is quite another matter. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has already been admitted as Exhibit P949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer do you have, Mr. Karadzic, for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had hoped to have until the end of today's proceedings, but I see that I'll have to accelerate. If I were to ask shorter questions and get shorter answers, I could manage. And leave you the 50-odd minutes that you said you needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break now for ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes, no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We had 30 minutes in -- during the first break. We will have 20 minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, a clarification on the record for the exhibit number for the diary will be D237. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Also, Mr. President, I will ask to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just will ask to clarify that the diary that's been admitted goes from the period of the 1st of March to the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's from 11th March -- could you give the date again. The first -- the beginning date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. 1 March to 11 May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have no objection to that, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now have P927 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, Colonel, I'd like to draw your attention to page 100 of the 21st of May where Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff asked you the following: "[In English] My last question is, Dr. Karadzic have control over these Bosnian Serb paramilitaries?" [Interpretation] And you were answer was: "[In English] Well, I always assumed that he did, because as -- as the conflict escalated, he seemed to be always in the presence of people who were armed who were close to him. Some of those were wearing the uniforms of JNA on occasions and sometimes they weren't. So it was my -- I suppose it was my interpretation or my view that as the leader of Bosnian Serbs, that he controlled or should have controlled over all aspects of the Bosnian Serbs, and that would include armed forces." [Interpretation] Let's clarify that a bit. We've already said that the escort I had was a police escort sent to me by our joint MUP and then our own MUP later on, but do you agree that when I was going to Belgrade with them or to some institutions that they had to wear civilian clothing, they had to be in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the details of the security that you would have had going to meetings, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm just referring to the comment you made that some of them weren't in uniform, but never mind. Can you now tell me --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or, rather, may we have on e-court P927 first, please. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then I'm going to ask you whether you can tell me here and now which --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not it. That's not the document I would want, I need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what paramilitary forces were they that I could control before the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about people who were armed, who were Bosnian Serbs; whether they were actually armed forces or not, I don't know because most of the time they weren't in uniform. So this is an assumption I have. But such was the amount of firing and conflict that going on in Sarajevo, that it would be naive for me to think that it was all Muslims attacking Serbs and there was no response. I'm mindful of the siege that took place in that city, but ... So I thought I had mentioned this yesterday, Mr. Karadzic, in relation to those people who were -- that you had protecting you. I don't know whether they were an armed, whether they were a unit of such, or whether they were just people who just had weapons who were giving you their protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was 8 to 12 people assigned to me by the police, but what I'm saying is that we agreed that each municipality had its Territorial Defence and that the president of the municipality was the commander of the Territorial Defence, and you accepted that and said that that was in keeping with the Law of Yugoslavia and Tito's Doctrine of All People's Defence. Now, do you consider that I could have controlled any Territorial Defence until the 12th of May in the municipalities, that I had a system of communications and the necessary authority, official authority, to be able to be in charge of those people?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I am saying is that as the leader of the Bosnian Serbs I would be my assumption that you as the leader would have had or should have had control over all armed and unarmed elements of Bosnian Serbs, whether they were armed or not. I'm not talking about -- and here I'm talking mainly about the city of Sarajevo where I was based and -- and where you were frequently present. So that's what I'm saying, that part of the authority of holding a position of leadership is to have control over those elements that are under your influence. And whether that be military or not, it's all the one to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have 65 ter 11591 next, please, and then we'll look at page 3 of that document. It's a report from the Secretary-General, 23.900, of the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, do you agree that up until the 12th of May I was the political leader of the Bosnian Serbs and that it was only on the 12th of May that I was elected to some state organ, that is to say, to the Presidency? Perhaps I was speaking too fast. This is what I asked you: Did you -- do you agree that I, until the 12th of May, 1992, was only the political leader without any state functions, state posts, public office, and that it was only on the 12th of May that I was elected to the Presidency and that I became the president of the Presidency elected at the Assembly on the 12th of May in Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from a state organ that may have been the case, but I have no doubt you had a huge influence over the actions of armed Bosnian Serbs in the city of Sarajevo. We can refer to the time that there was a firing coming from the Holiday Inn hotel, and there were many other instances. So I do not accept that you had no influence over armed Serb elements in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who and when shot from the Holiday Inn, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about a period after the referendum results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know, Colonel, that there was shooting from the Unis tower and that the Serbs wouldn't have dared to shoot with 50.000 Muslim demonstrators, that Juka Prazina did the shooting in order to create chaos? And we have footage of that, Colonel. So how can you maintain that it was a Serb shooting from the Holiday Inn? Do you have proof or evidence to show that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have proof or evidence but I'm saying that that is something that was generally accepted. The point I'm trying to get across here is that you were the leader of the Bosnian Serbs, you had a huge amount of influence in the city, and therefore it is my belief that you had influence over armed elements of Serbs in that city. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's your opinion and belief, but I'm asking for your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's have page 3 of this document that's an exhibit already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to focus on the end of paragraph 5 where it says: "There will leave -- Mr. Goulding had informed the Secretary-General --" Well, let's start this way: "Further concern has been caused by the decision of the Belgrade authorities to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina [In English] by May the 18th, all JNA personnel who are not citizens of that republic. This will leave in Bosnia-Herzegovina, without effective political control, as many as 50.000 mostly Serb troops and their weapons. They are likely to be taken over by the Serb party." [Interpretation] So this was reported on on the 12th of May, Colonel. And from this it clearly follows that the Serb side, up until then, did not have political control over the army and that for the time being it would not have. And I claim that the decision to form an army was taken on the 12th of May coming into force as of the 20th of May. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I do know that you made a statement to the effect that there would be an army raised. We're not talking here about an army. We're talking about armed Bosnian Serbs that, in my view, were under your control and under your influence. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have proof of that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I have service in the Republic of Bosnia, and I'm -- I'm -- I'm rather anxious here about giving my opinion about anything, because you've always looked for facts, but when you're given a position of responsibility, you carry out certain acts and then you're asked to make a summary and your views and your recommendations and your conclusions, and I've always attempted to do that. If you don't accept those as my conclusions, that is your privilege.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Colonel, do you make the difference between a party function and a public function, state function? Is there any -- is there a differentiation there be it the head of a political party, the political leader, who, only on the 12th of May, became part of the official state structure? Do you make that difference?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a difference. I repeat again that in my view you had an influence over the actions of Bosnian Serbs in the city of Sarajevo who were armed. That is my conclusion. You may accept it or you may not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, a conclusion is one thing; a belief is another. Now, what strings could I pull for organising the self-organised people of the local community and Territorial Defence? How could I command them and who could I command them? How could I put this into practice, sitting in the Holiday Inn negotiating with you, with Izetbegovic, with Kukanjac, how would I have been able to do that then?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I have no evidence of it, but I assume you would have a people who would have done that on your behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's leave your assumptions to one side. We'll have a glass of wine after these proceedings and then we can assume all we like. But would you focus on paragraph 7 now of this report by the Secretary-General. Who killed this representative of your mission?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I'll have a look at that. Yes. I was aware of the fact that a member of the monitor mission was killed near Mostar. He was from Belgium, I think. But I have no -- I have no -- I have no details of how it happened or who did it. Is this -- is this what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we've finished with this document. Now, Colonel, the next thing I want to address is not on e-court, but I'm just going to read it out to you. It dates to 1994, the numerical state of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. Officers, 18.803; and soldiers, 228.000; non-commissioned officers, 24.000; which makes a total of 271.000. Yes, 271.000, and I've been asked to speak slower. Anyway, Colonel, can you tell me where these 18.803 officers were schooled and educated and the 24.263 non-commissioned officers? Were they officers and non-commissioned officers of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And which other army could they have belonged to?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what other army they could belong to. I assume most of them came from the JNA, but if you're talking to the numerical state of the Bosnian Serb Army as in -- sorry, the not the Bosnian Serb Army, the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army as in those elements that were not Serb, a number of 18.800 officers and 228.000 men and 24 [sic] non-commissioned officers seems a huge number to me, so I really don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic was reading from a document, but we don't have that document. Nobody else has this document. So I wonder what -- what value it is when he reads from an unknown source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I agree. When you put the document, you should introduce the foundation of the document. I take it you're going to do that. If you could tell us what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the Muslim review of the replenishment of the BH Army on the 1st of November, 1994. I will present that and tender it on another occasion because the Colonel wasn't there at the time. I'd just like to show him that on that day they had almost 300.000 soldiers and officers, all of whom were officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, and the soldiers were the reservists of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So I'm putting that to you Colonel and asking you the question that I asked you a moment ago. Do you accept the fact that the Yugoslav People's Army was the mother of all the republican armies that came into being after the disintegration of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I agree that the JNA was the federal army which represented all of the republics. The figure of these -- these Bosnian-Herzegovinian army at that time with that amount of officers, non-commissioned officers and men, I have no idea. I don't know how they were constituted of where they came from or who trained them or what percentage would have come from the federal army. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to call up another document on the ELMO. Well, I'm not going to tender it today. I'd just like you, Colonel, to have a look at it, and I'd like us to objectivise, that is to say, to see what forces the parties in Bosnia had at there are disposal. And in saying that I want to say that the Muslim side had more than two and a half times more soldiers than the Serbs did and that from the very beginning they were ready for war, that they were well armed, especially after they left the JNA barracks. And now, as I say, I'm going to put this document on the ELMO for you to look at, but I'm not going to tender it today. Just to give you an idea of the actions launched by the 2nd Corps of the BH Army during the period you were there, that is to say, up until the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you put it to the witness, tell us what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is -- well, the number of the document on the top is 020 -- can you lower it down? 0203-1418. It's a Prosecution document. And the title is a list of -- can we see the top. Yes. Thank you. A list of combat operations conducted in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's the Tuzla Corps, isn't it? The Tuzla Corps; right, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't know that Tuzla had a corps, the 2nd JNA corps -- or, rather, BH Army Corps?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know it had a corps, but I don't -- I don't understand the title of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's an ERN number at the top. It's one we were disclosed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm talking about the actual document itself, not the number that's on it. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The title is the following: "List of combat actions," BD is combat actions, "carried out in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps from 1992 to 1995." So I have marked in red only those offensives that were launched while you were there. Number 5, the attack on Cer, for example. That took place on the 26th of April. Otherwise, from the beginning, the defence that we have, Becirevic Defence, Potocari Defence, an ambush there, Snagovo, attack on Cer. So number 5, listed under number 5. Then under number 8, attack on Setici. And then it says, Serb Setici in Zvornik - there's the Muslim Setici in Zvornik, but they attacked the Serb Setici, Zvornik, on the 1st of May. Then we come to number 13, a diversion at Srpski Nezuk. You have a Muslim village and a Serb village there. The Muslim made up of the initial Serb village. But it's all in Zvornik municipality. Then we have the attack on the village of Sapna -- and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is this, Your Excellency, while the Colonel was in the area, the 2nd Corps of the BH Army, fully ready and prepared, launched a number of armed operations, many of which were offensives, offensive, and I want to show the Colonel that the Muslims weren't helpless and attacked. They did have their own army, and they did launch combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's -- and this lists all the actions undertaken by the 2nd Corps, Colonel, while you yourself were there.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Karadzic, is this document that was made up by the official JNA Army or by the army that you're calling the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The army which I called and which was the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I also refer to it as the Muslim Army because there were a negligible number of Serbs and Croats in it. This is the corps of the officially called Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which, from the first day, had offensive combat actions. And Mr. Martin Bell informed you about the departure of civilians from Zvornik. And you can see that in Zvornik and around Zvornik fierce fighting was being carried out and that the Tuzla Corps was taking parted in them. My question is: Did you know that the corps from Tuzla was in readiness from the 1st of April to go into action, the Muslim Corps from Tuzla, from the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please scroll down to number 12 to see how many offensive actions this corps carried out. Can you move the page a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What point is there if the witness has no -- knows nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, the Colonel should know. He was the head of the monitor mission. He was in Krajina, in Derventa. If I had time, I would show him the massacres around Derventa of the Serbian population at the time that he was there. He should know that the Muslim army was numerous and well armed and that already as of the 4th of April it was capable of conducting extensive combat actions. And if he knows, this is quite significant information; and if he doesn't know, then by his own admission he should state that he was not highly enough placed to know about these things and then we would need to listen to what his superior would have to say. He -- we have a reference that he was in Zvornik and the -- Zvornik is in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Instead of reading out the document, put your specific questions one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I put the question and I received an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My thesis is that the Muslim army had plenty of soldiers and weapons as of the 4th of April, 1992, to embark on extensive offensive actions, and this is what this document indicates. Did you know that? You said that you didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I do have a translation of this document here, and what we hear here from Mr. Karadzic is a misrepresentation. Because looking at the document and the English version, it's -- I haven't counted it, but I would say it's mostly defence of certain villages. And it's not, as it is shown here, offensive actions throughout. If we continue to use this document, I would rather think that we should also have the English version of it because it's definitely -- it gives it a different character, at least the actions that are referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, that's very helpful. But I think we almost exhausted this topic. Would you like to bring up the English translation and pursue further on this line?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have to insist any more. I just wanted to say that I marked the assault actions. Of course, there were defensive actions as well, but the entire document you will see later I limited myself up until the 12th of May. But the entire document will indicate that they attacked much more than they defended themselves. I state that it is not correct that the Muslims were disorganised and unarmed because on the 4th of April this corps began to undertake actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My second question, Colonel, is this: Do you know that Mr. Izetbegovic declared a general call-up on the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you accept that you did not receive complete information from Mr. Bell about the events in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether the information was complete or not. He came to me about a particular incident, and that -- that's all. In relation to this document here, I did a survey of all the senior JNA commanders in Bosnia, and none of these issues were brought up by them when I met these commanders. There were general issues. The JNA army commanders were concerned about the future stability of the republic, but when I made myself available to all of them, I met the commander, I think his name was Djeneral Jankovic, up in Tuzla in this area and none of these matters were brought to my attention at that meeting. So I'm not denying that they took place, I just have no knowledge of it and I don't have any reports on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Colonel, as for the general call-up, we are talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I thought -- that's an error there on my part. I thought we were talking about the decision by the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To -- to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic's declaration of a general call-up. You answered yes to the question of whether it was on the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm actual not aware of that instance. I'm sorry. I thought Mr. Karadzic was referring to the declaration by the president that there would not be a mobilisation of -- by the JNA. That's my error. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you know that Izetbegovic had declared the general mobilisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina of the Territorial Defence the police and everything on the 4th in the evening?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall he making an appeal for -- for call-ups, but I don't know -- I don't recall when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For your information, Serbian members of the Presidency, Plavsic and Koljevic, objected to that, and could not have called for a general mobilisation without their agreement. I would now like to call up one of your reports of the 7th of May when you informed Ambassador Cutileiro about the events in Mostar. There were two UNPROFOR members in Mostar who were wounded at the time, one of them seriously. And then you go on to say -- this is an associate of yours, Boban HDZ.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D018 -- 1D01281, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are informing here that Boban and Karadzic have reached an agreement [In English] at a meeting concerning the resolution of all the differences between the two nations through conciliatory means including the territorial delimitation and at the auspice of the European Community. They reassured firmly the agreement of principles defined in the conference in Lisbon. There is no further reasons for the continuation of armed conflict between the Serbs and the Croats. The territorial delimitation between the -- between the nations will be made until the 15th of May. Cease-fire will be decreed from today, 2400 hours." [Interpretation] Do you remember these events and this report?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the way back from Lisbon, Mr. Boban and I met in Graz, and we concluded, in accordance with the conference and the call by Mr. Carrington, that we should accept the working map and that there was no point in fighting over a small number of disputed territories. You don't remember that, but I think this was sent while you were still there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the EC monitor mission, and it's from head of mission. The head of the mission was based in Zagreb, Ambassador Salguero. So I have no knowledge of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this document accepted? I would like to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Considering this document has come from the organisation the witness belonged to and then there's no doubt as to the authenticity, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D238, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D01247.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, let me inform you that this Djeneral Jankovic whom you've mentioned is informing on the 3rd of April about events up to the 3rd of April and on the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no translation, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is no translation, but I am going to read it to you. We can see here in paragraph 3 that the paramilitary formations from the direction of the village of Koraci [phoen] opened fire at the JNA units located in the Kostrec and Barice villages. Then in the next paragraph it says one of our soldiers was killed in the conflict. This is before the official beginning of the war. Then it goes on to say in the last paragraph on the first page: "On the 3rd of April, 1992, a meeting was held in Tuzla of the council for national defence." I think you have been given the minutes from the meeting. At 1700 hours also, a meeting was called of the Municipal Assembly of Tuzla on the political security situation in the territory of the SO Tuzla to which our representative was not invited. On the 3rd of April there was also a meeting on the political security situation in the municipality of Doboj which was attended by the commander of the 6th Militarised Brigade on the territory and so on and so forth. In the territory of the municipality of Brcko, the reserve police forces had been called up and police stations have been set up in certain village settlements. Leaders of national parties are carrying out intense preparations for new conflicts. Arms are being publicly distributed to members of the SDA at several public places. At 1500 hours on the 3rd of April, weapons were distributed to SDA members in the village of Ciljuge, the Zivinice municipality near Dzamir [phoen]. And these men were supposed to move towards Bijeljina in the course of the 3rd and 4th of April, 1992. So you mentioned the general who was not sympathetic towards us at all. He was an old-fashioned general, against all national parties and against the multi-party system, but here his soldiers are getting killed before the beginning of the war, and he's informing his command about what was going on there. I am -- I have to admit to you that we Serbs did not know how to sell our misfortunes very well, but do you accept that there were tensions, that it was very tense around Tuzla, even though former Communists were in power in and around Tuzla at that time?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason not to accept the content of this report by the general. I have no detailed knowledge of each of the incidents he's referring to, but I have no reason to have any objection to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would I like to tender this document for identification only.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have actually a translation, because it is a duplicate of an exhibit that the Prosecution actually also wanted to bring forward at some point in time, and it's 0 -- 07089. And we do have a translation, and it should be available through e-court under that number. And there is no objection to tendering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 07089 will be admitted as Exhibit D239.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karadzic, you have to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D225 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you remember what the confrontation line was like? What did it look like at the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you'd have to be more specific as to the time. I was -- I was there for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The conflict began on the 6th of April on our side, although the conflicts began before. But let's say from the 6th of April until the 12th of May, what did the demarcation line look like or the line of confrontation; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see these blue areas marking the areas with a pronounced Serb majority?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the map in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the demarcation line mostly followed the outlines of these blue areas?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to any great extent. In general detail, yes, but the monitor mission wasn't in any way involved in making out detailed divisions of territories depending on their ethnic percentages. It was something we did not want to get involved in, because then, as I had mentioned before, we stayed away from internal borders in opstina, et cetera, et cetera. In other words, most of our -- most of our work was done in actually speaking with people, speaking with political groups, and didn't have very much to do with maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that what was referred to in the war as Republika Srpska was mostly limited to these areas that are represented here in blue? Was that Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- in general terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D01275, please. 1D01275.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is a document of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 29th of April. Colonel, do you see this conversation between -- in the English it says the 28th of August, 1992, but I believe, actually, it's April according to the contents. By the contents, I believe that it is April. Now, let's see. This General Siber is speaking with Hosen. Hosen is probably an UNPROFOR officer. And it says here three French soldiers were seriously wounded in Nedzarici today. One is in critical condition, and the second one lost an eye. And then later, 500 metres away from our facilities, they are not being observed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is kindly asked to point to the interpreters where he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters were not able to follow your reading, so could you kindly indicate what part -- from what part you are reading and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am reading from the middle of the first page. "... in Nedzarici. That is not a game. That is not a game. I'm very open. I have come to help as much as I can. The desire of the United Nations in term of establishing the peace should be achieved. Guns should be silenced. And the beautiful song of peace should be heard." And so on and so forth. And then a few sentences later: "Three French soldiers were seriously wounded in Nedzarici today."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Nedzarici is Serbian settlement next to Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say are --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we zoom down the page to see the bottom of the English page. Around about "500 metres." Can we see the English better, please. You can -- that's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "[In English] In relation -- [Interpretation] In relation to the 500 distance from our facilities, it is not respected." And r. Hosen is the person speaking. "Three days ago, some mortars were active near the PTT building. The Serbs responded and hit our building, but luckily there were no casualties. I'm asking for your co-operation and understanding. Please order a 500 metre distance from our facilities." And Siber says: "We've already issued that order." And then Hosen goes on to say: "We received this from London -- the following from London."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page for the English page, next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "In London we got from the Serbs as well guarantees that within 96 hours they would allow UNPROFOR access to all locations of heavy artillery around Sarajevo. I expect that you will provide us with that as well." Now, you mentioned the PTT building, Colonel, and I'm telling you that this was what happened all the time, that Muslim artillery and mortars would come close up to the United Nations installations and open fire on them. And then when we respond, they accuse us and blame us. Now, in the previous paragraph it said that in Nedzarici the United Nations were repairing installations, gas installations and other things that everybody needed including the Muslims, whereas the Muslims shot at a Serb settlement and wounded three French soldiers. Now, do you know about this formula for behaviour on the part of the Muslim army? They bring their weapons close up to UN installations and then open fire as this gentleman, Mr. Hosen, says. And he's asking them to keep a distance of 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from my experience of severing with the United Nations as a military officer that parties to a conflict have always used -- has often used a United Nations position in which to launch fire at their enemies so that the enemy doesn't want to respond by firing into a United Nations position. That's been something that's been done by all sides in most of the countries that I have served in with the United Nations. This particular document I'm for the familiar with. I don't know who the Hosen is. You say he may be a general of the United Nations, I don't know. This is something that might be better taken up with respect with somebody who served with the United Nations and UNPROFOR. I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not only speaking about that particular case, but the general formula according to which they acted. And did the Serb side do anything like that during the war? You said the Serb side -- you said the various sides, but I claiming that the Serb side didn't. Now, the last document - I'd like to tender this document - but let's see what the Serb police has to say and the information it put out by looking at the next document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness didn't have anything to comment upon. We will not admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the witness did say earlier on that the Serbs shooted at the PTT building without reason. That what said a long time ago and in the statement. And I said that there was every reason. It wasn't that there wasn't a reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will have another opportunity to introduce evidence. So was that your last examination -- question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to show another Serb police document on this same event to see -- to show that the two things are identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness was not able to answer the question about the incident you are referring to, there's no point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, then, my last question: Looking at this document and taking into account the fact that I'm speaking about a pattern of behaviour, not individual incidents, do you exclude the possibility that the Muslim side used this war ruse, especially with respect to the PTT building but also in respect of other UN installations?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in the PTT building, it was the headquarters of the United Nations UNPROFOR operation. They might be in a much better position to answer that than I would. I do know that mortar bombs fired at the building when I was in the middle of trying to negotiate a cease-fire. Who exactly fired those, I don't know. The general feeling at the time, they were coming from high positions on the outskirts of Sarajevo which would have led one to suspect it was coming from Bosnian Serb positions. But I have to say to you that I -- I don't have any evidence of this. Rather, I have a suspicion and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Before the Prosecution asks some questions in redirect, Judge Baird has some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, I would like your assistance in a particular area, and I shall direct your attention to the evidence that was given yesterday. Now, you stated in answer to Dr. Karadzic, he asked you: "Did you understand that there were discrimination in rent, one price for the Muslims and another for the Serbs?" And your answer was: "That was my understanding of that meeting." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
