utterances.text: Yes. And he then asks you: "And did you then check that out with the Serbs? Did you ask the mayor about that and check it out?" And your reply was: "I did not bring it up with the mayor, and I did not check it out."

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my recollection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, my question, Colonel, is did you -- is there any reason at all why you didn't check it out?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of the points that were brought to our attention at the various meetings, we would have tried to discuss those at the next highest level. I can't recall whether or not I brought up that specific point with the mayor. It is 18 years. And rather than say I did, I probably said, Well, maybe I didn't. But there were many issues that were brought up around that time. What we were attempting to do was we were attempting to bring the concerns of one side to the attention of the authorities, to find out if they would have a response. So the answer is, I can't answer that question, Your Honour, because I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to have the 65 ter number 07868 brought up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Colonel, you discussed with Dr. Karadzic a letter that Karadzic sent to Cutileiro on the 5th of June, 1992, and you said that you do not remember this and you do not know about this. Now, we have now on the e-court -- we have the answer, as it says here: "Thank you for your letter of the 5th of June." It's the answer of Cutileiro on the 12th of June, and it refers here in the -- in the first paragraph it refers to Lord Carrington and his views, and it's stated here: "I firmly believe that the only way to bring peace to Bosnia and Herzegovina is through negotiations." And a lit bit further down in that paragraph: "Territorial claims which have been pursued by force are totally unacceptable." Is that what the views of Lord Carrington were at that time?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And now to the last paragraph. Cutileiro writes here as follows: "Let me add one thing. Referring to the last paragraph of your letter, the EC has not made any promises to you. What happened, as you well know, is that talks on future constitutional arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina among the three main political parties (Muslim, Serb, and Croat) under my chairmanship, were established by Lord Carrington and in early -- in early February. On 18th March, we reached agreement on a set of principles. The validity of that agreement, however, can only be upheld if borders and competences of the constituent units be defined by negotiated consensus and not by force, and if ethnically cleansed territories be restored to their antebellum ethnical composition. I am sure you relies that it is in your interest to do everything from your side to help achieve those results." Do you have any further comment on this, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would say that, as I had mentioned before, I was aware that there was to be the elements of agreement, which was dated to the 18th of March, the content of which I certainly was not aware of. So this probably reinforces what Mr. Cutileiro was saying, which I have no reason to -- to oppose. But I personally had not been involved in those negotiations and, therefore, I have -- I have no definite views on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can I now, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit number ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Exhibit P952.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could we now have Exhibit 65 ter 12051, the first page both in the English and the B/C/S, brought up.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Colonel, yesterday Dr. Karadzic on several occasions addressed with you the existence or nonexistence of a Bosnian Serb Army before the official establishment of the VRS and before the withdrawal of the JNA in May 1992, and he put to you - and I'm referring here to page transcript page 2890, line 4 - he put to you the following: "You accept that up until the 20th of May the Bosnian Serbs were under the command of the JNA or of their own municipal territory organisation while during the same time the Muslims had their own armed formations." Looking at the first page here, it -- it is a press report on Srpska "Oslobodjenje" titled "Happy Birthday, Republic," and it's an interview that Radovan Karadzic gave on the 6th of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we please have page 3 in the English, and page 1 of the B/C/S remains.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the -- in the first paragraph -- let me just ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Page 3. Is that page 3 in the English?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the first -- in the first paragraph it says -- and Dr. Karadzic is quoted as saying: "Of course, Republika Srpska is a reality, the same as the Republic of Serbian Krajina is a reality, and we believe that these are just steps in creation of a single Serbian state." Colonel, this notion of a single Serbian state, is this something that you heard being mentioned during meetings or conferences?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the -- the general feeling at these conferences was that the overall objective of Serbs was to join physically the territories that the Serbs controlled in Bosnia to the territory of Serbia to create a Greater Serbia. That was the general understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And further on that same page - and it is page 2 in the -- in the B/C/S - further down in this -- in the English Dr. Karadzic is quoted as saying: "We had a list of the actions and steps to take, but we always waited for the Muslims to make a mistake, and after they made one, we created a union of municipalities and the Serbian autonomous areas next, followed by the regions, and eventually our Assembly, and finally republic. Every time that the Muslim and Croat -- Croatian representatives told us that we were breaking up former Bosnia and Herzegovina, we replied that our actions were only in response to their mistakes and their aggression against our political rights." Colonel, is that consistent with the information that you had during your term of office?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And now if we go to page 4 of the English, and it's -- it remains to be page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I -- I'm reading now another of the quotes: "The Serbian Democratic Party also endured the armed struggle in a superior manner. It was the first time that the people knew what was in store for them. With such well-organised defence, the majority of our people has been saved, and lines towards the enemy were established. We should always remember that the people themselves and the SDS fought and set up the front lines in 45 days from 5th of April to 20th May while our army was still being established. Eventually, of course, this army became non-Partisan, but we did not want to appoint any SDS commissioners to it because we relied on the patriotism of each of our officers and soldiers." Colonel, is this consistent what -- with what you saw and what you have referred to before during your term of office?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- one other point. One other point. Sorry. Can we again have the Exhibit 11591. Oh, I forgot. I would like to have this -- this document admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P953, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And, again, the item 11591, the 65 ter. That was already admitted, but now it's the further report -- no, that's the wrong. It should be the further report of the Secretary-General of 12 May 1992. It's item 11591, 65 ter. It has a P number. 937, sorry. 937. And I would like to have page 3 and -- page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that's the paragraph number 5 on top of it that you just discussed with Dr. Karadzic. When we look at it, it says here: "Further concern has been caused by the decision of the Belgrade authorities to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina by 18 May all JNA personnel who are not citizens of that republic." And then the next sentence: "This will leave in Bosnia-Herzegovina without effective political control as many as 50 [sic] mostly Serb troops ..." Does this relate to the form JNA troops or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it would relate to those members of the JNA who were Serbs and were from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this concludes the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Just one question, Colonel Doyle, just to satisfy my own curiosity. Were you an infantry officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I thought you were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concludes your testimony, Colonel Doyle. Thank you for your coming yet again to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the Court Deputy is able to do it without the assistance of the usher. Can you draw up the exhibit number D324? No, it's not -- or it may be -- might have been D235. Where we can find the word "siege," for which the exact translation should have been "encirclement," according to the accused? I think it was page 5 in the e-court. Yes. In the middle of the page. Along with "task," we can see the word "siege of Sarajevo." And can you go back to page 3 there. In the "I have decided" column or the "Operation Objectives," third paragraph, Mladic says: "Keep Sarajevo from the -- under blockade." So with the -- if the Court Deputy would relay with the CLSS to find out what words in B/C/S were used for the "siege" and "blockade" and compare them with the transcript of 19th of May as well as 27th of May when the -- Mr. Karadzic tried to explain the difference between the "encirclement" and "siege," and I'd like to know what B/C/S words were used at those times. So I would like the CLSS to produce a written memo on those things and file it. There are several matters, administrative matters, to deal with. I'll begin with some minor things. There's a motion from the Prosecution to add a witness, Amir Begic, to its witness list. And I take it there is no opposition from the Defence, but there is a request from the Defence that Prosecution would call the witness after the summer recess. Do you have any position?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we can accommodate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that understanding, we'll -- your motion is granted. And there are two further motions: Leave to reply; one in relation to the videolink testimony, and the other related to certain protective measures. So they are granted. And this relates to the -- the motion from the accused for extension and adjournment: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber has received a request from you for an extension of time to respond to the Prosecution's second motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list which pertains to the Mladic notebook. We have also taken into account the Prosecution's response to that request filed today. The Chamber considers some extension of time is appropriate for you to prepare your response to the motion and that an addition two weeks is sufficient. You are, therefore, required to file your response to the Prosecution motion, if any, by 14 June 2010. You have also requested that the Chamber adjourn the trial proceedings for a period of 30 days to allow you to study the Mladic notebooks which were disclosed to you in your own language first on 12th of April, 2010, and determine their impact on your cross-examination of the upcoming Prosecution witnesses. The Prosecution has stated its opposition to this request. Having considered all the submissions made, the Chamber finds that it is not necessary nor in the interest of justice to adjourn the trial proceedings at this time. As we have previously stated, you have had sufficient time to prepare your cross-examination of the Prosecution's witnesses and have been on notice of the witnesses to be called in this initial phase of the trial for many months now. If after reviewing the notebooks that have been disclosed to you or indeed any other material recently disclosed by the Prosecution you determine that there are additional questions you would wish to put to a particular witness on cross-examination, you may make the appropriate application to the Chamber. With regard to the majority of the upcoming witnesses, the Chamber is convinced that this remedy would suffice. We will, therefore, deny your motion for an adjournment at the present time. Having said that, the Chamber would like to encourage the Prosecution to rethink its order of upcoming witnesses and suggests that it would be appropriate to move Witness KDZ88 down the schedule so that this evidence might be heard a little later in the proceedings after the accused has had a little more time to analyse the notebooks disclosed to him on 12th of April. Given the expected content of KDZ88's evidence, it seems to the Chamber that such a rescheduling will be prudent. The last matter, last agenda that I have, relates to your conduct of your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic. In relation to that, I would like to make some comments on behalf of the Chamber concerning the manner in which you are conducting your cross-examination in general. Before your cross-examination of the very first witness, I told you that the Chamber did not consider your time estimate for cross-examination of the initial witnesses to be realistic or reasonable. The Chamber has, nonetheless, given you significant latitude to conduct your cross-examinations in the way you consider most appropriate and has granted extensive time to you to do so. This is partly because we recognise that you are not a trained lawyer and that effective cross-examination can be a difficult skill to master. Asking open questions or multiple questions in cross-examination is not only a poor technique but is not likely to be effective. Closed, direct questions put one at a time are both more effective and in general more likely to generate more concise and precise answers. You should also note that it is only the answers of the witness to your questions that amount to evidence as well as the documents or parts thereof that the witness adopts and which are admitted into evidence. Reading out the whole or large parts of a document into the transcript is a time-consuming procedure which does not have the effect of turning the transcripted parts into evidence if the document is not ultimately admitted. It's a far better use of time to formulate the questions from the document and only resort to the document if necessary to contradict the witness's answer. You have received such advice repeatedly from the Bench about how to more effectively conduct your cross-examination as well as warnings not to make statements and comments, not to read out extensive passages from documents, but, rather, to show documents to the witnesses and ask pointed questions in relation to them and not to put questions to witnesses about matters which they have stated they have no knowledge of. Despite our efforts in this regard, and I hope also the efforts of your own legal advisors, to guide you, the Chamber is concerned that you are not making more effective use of your time for your cross-examination. We are also concerned again by the time estimate you have recently given for the next nine witnesses. The Chamber is therefore contemplating setting time limits on your cross-examination of each witness, which we will determine on a witness-by-witness basis, and which you will be required to comply with unless you can show good cause why additional time is necessary. Should you not demonstrate during your cross-examination of the next witnesses that you are taking seriously our advice, the Chamber will begin to impose such time limits. Having said this, the Chamber is of the view, based on the time you have already used for cross-examination of Mr. Van Lynden, your own estimate of how much additional time you need with him and on the nature and content of Mr. Van Lynden's evidence, that you should be able to complete your cross-examination of him within two hours. The Trial Chamber's primary task is to ensure a fair trial, but that entails fairness for everyone involved, and undue delay is not consonant with fairness. We will rise for today. We will resume again on Monday afternoon at 2.15. Everybody have a good weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 31st day of May, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
